modalities.name: Plain Sensation Words
modalities.tagline: Your felt sense in plain body words, right now, on your own.
modalities.whatItIs: Plain Sensation Words is a new, untested concept that takes Focusing further away from guided imagery work. You attend to the vague bodily sense of your situation right now, but describe it only in plain sensation words such as tight, warm or heavy, with no pictures, stories or memories.
modalities.coreIdea: Staying with what the body is doing in the present, without turning it into images or history, may let a situation be felt freshly.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone, sit or lie down for 10 to 15 minutes and ask how a current situation feels in your body right now. Each time a word comes, check that it names a sensation (pressure, flutter, ache) rather than a picture or a memory, and let the sensation be as it is without asking it to change.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a simple self-led practice and find imagery or digging into the past tiring.
modalities.cautions: Even plain body attention can bring up strong feelings, so open your eyes or stop if it becomes too much. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should work with a qualified therapist, and this untested idea is not a substitute for treatment.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Plain Sensation Words. You check how a situation feels in your body right now and describe it only in plain words like tight or warm. No images, no backstory. A simple, solo way to get clearer on what you feel.

modalities.name: How This Place Feels
modalities.tagline: Sense how the place you are in sits in your body.
modalities.whatItIs: How This Place Feels is a new concept that moves Focusing away from therapies built around inner parts and imagined figures, toward the real place you are in. Alone, you let a felt sense form of being in this particular room, street or building right now, and listen to what it says about your life there.
modalities.coreIdea: The places we spend time in carry a bodily feel of their own, and sensing it directly may show what a workplace, home or habit is really like for you.
modalities.whatYouDo: Wherever you are, a kitchen, an office or a bus, sit for 10 minutes with your eyes open, take in the space and ask "what is it like for me to be here?" Wait for a bodily answer (cramped, warm, buzzing, flat), find a word that fits and let it be, without deciding anything.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a quick, self-led way to notice how their surroundings affect them, for example before deciding whether to change jobs, rooms or routines.
modalities.cautions: Some places hold hard associations, so you can stop the exercise or leave the place if it stirs too much. It is an untested idea, and if a home or workplace feels unsafe, practical help and support matter more than any inner practice.
modalities.tweet: New concept: How This Place Feels. Wherever you are, kitchen, office or bus, pause and ask what it's like for your body to be here, then find one word that fits. A quick, solo way to notice how your surroundings sit with you.

modalities.name: Let the Body Choose
modalities.tagline: No topic, no steps, no goal: the body sets the agenda.
modalities.whatItIs: Let the Body Choose is a new concept that strips Focusing of its steps and goals, moving it as far as possible from structured, agenda-led therapy. You pick no topic in advance; you lie down, wait, and whatever the body brings forward becomes the session.
modalities.coreIdea: Trusting the body to choose what needs attention, with no agenda and no aim to change it, may surface concerns a planned session would skip.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down somewhere quiet for 20 to 30 minutes with no topic and no technique. Wait until some bodily sense stands out and keep it company without trying to name or change it; if words or images arrive, welcome them, but they are not required.
modalities.whoItsFor: People worn out by worksheets, goals and self-improvement plans who want an open, body-led way to listen to themselves.
modalities.cautions: Without structure, unexpected feelings or memories can surface, so keep the freedom to sit up, open your eyes and stop. Anyone with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or suicidal thoughts should use it only with a qualified therapist, and it is an untested idea rather than a treatment.
modalities.tweet: What if your body set the agenda? Let the Body Choose is a new idea: lie down with no topic, no steps and no goal, and keep company with whatever sense stands out. For people tired of worksheets and self-improvement plans.

modalities.name: How Old Is This
modalities.tagline: Stay inside a feeling and sense how long you have known it.
modalities.whatItIs: How Old Is This is a speculative practice that moves Focusing away from action plans and from stepping back to watch your thoughts. Instead of observing a feeling from a distance and turning it into a next step, you let yourself be fully inside its bodily sense and gently notice whether it feels new or long familiar.
modalities.coreIdea: Many bodily feelings carry a sense of age, and simply sensing how familiar a feeling is, without acting on it, may give it room to be understood.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone, sit or lie down for about 20 minutes, let the bodily sense of a current feeling fill your attention, and stay inside it rather than watching it. Then quietly ask "how old does this feel?", receive whatever comes (a year, a place or just "very old"), and finish without making any plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice the same feelings returning and want a calm, self-led way to sense where they come from without analyzing them.
modalities.cautions: Asking about the age of a feeling can bring old memories forward, so go slowly, stop if it gets intense, and work with a trauma-trained therapist if painful memories keep surfacing. It is an untested concept, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Ever had a feeling that seems older than the situation? New concept: How Old Is This. You stay inside a feeling's bodily sense and simply ask how old it feels, with no action plan. A quiet way to sense where your patterns come from.

modalities.name: Which Rest Is Needed
modalities.tagline: Sense what kind of rest your body is asking for right now.
modalities.whatItIs: Which Rest Is Needed is a speculative practice that moves Focusing far from therapies that dig for the hidden emotional reason behind a symptom, toward a plain, present question. When you feel drained, you let the body's felt sense show what kind of rest it wants, such as sleep, movement, quiet, company or play, rather than asking why you are drained.
modalities.coreIdea: Tiredness comes in different kinds, and the body may know which rest would help before the mind does.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone, lie down for 10 minutes and notice the felt quality of your tiredness: heavy, buzzy, empty or restless. Then try each option in turn ("a nap?", "a walk?", "a call with a friend?", "silence?"), notice which one the body leans toward and, if you can, give yourself that one.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who rest the same way every time, such as scrolling or sleeping, and still feel tired.
modalities.cautions: Ongoing exhaustion can be a sign of illness, poor sleep or depression, so check with a doctor if it persists. It is an untested idea and does not replace medical advice.
modalities.tweet: Tired but not sure what would help? New concept: Which Rest Is Needed. Lie down, feel the kind of tired you are, then try each option (a nap, a walk, a friend, silence) and notice which one your body leans toward.

modalities.name: Fitting Image Pairs
modalities.tagline: Two friends take turns finding the image that fits a feeling.
modalities.whatItIs: Fitting Image Pairs is a new concept that moves Focusing away from body exercises and toward images and words. Two people take turns: the explorer lets the felt sense of a situation show up as a metaphor (a kind of weather, a place, an object) while the other listens and reflects it back.
modalities.coreIdea: A well-fitting metaphor can hold a vague feeling better than a list of sensations, and checking that it fits may open the situation up.
modalities.whatYouDo: Meet a trusted partner for about 40 minutes and take turns of 15 to 20 minutes each. The explorer asks "if this situation were weather or a place, what would it be?" and checks the image against their inner sense until it fits, while the listener only repeats back the images and adds no advice.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find body sensations hard to read but think easily in pictures, and who like exploring with a friend.
modalities.cautions: Images can lead into painful memories, so either partner can pause or stop at any time, and listeners should not interpret or push. People with severe trauma, psychosis or dissociation should explore with a qualified therapist; it is an untested idea, not therapy.
modalities.tweet: If your week were weather, what would it be? Fitting Image Pairs is a new idea: two friends take turns finding the image that fits a vague feeling, and the listener just reflects it back. For people who think in pictures more than sensations.

modalities.name: Crossroads Body Check
modalities.tagline: A ten-minute, do-it-yourself way to include your gut in decisions.
modalities.whatItIs: Crossroads Body Check is a speculative, self-run practice that pushes Focusing away from coach-led depth work and toward everyday use. When you face a choice, you hold each option in mind in turn, notice the bodily sense each one brings, and weigh that alongside your usual reasoning.
modalities.coreIdea: The body often registers a choice before the mind can explain it, and a short, repeatable check can bring that information into ordinary decisions.
modalities.whatYouDo: Write down two or three options, then for each one sit for two or three minutes, imagine having chosen it and notice the felt sense (open, heavy, jittery, light). Jot one word for each, compare the words with your reasons, and decide on one small next step.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get stuck going back and forth on decisions and want a quick, structured way to include how they feel, without needing a coach.
modalities.cautions: A felt sense is information, not a verdict, so weigh it with facts and advice, especially for money, health or legal decisions. It is a new, untested practice, and a life crisis calls for support from people you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: Stuck between two choices? New concept: Crossroads Body Check. Picture having chosen each option, notice how your body responds, jot one word, then weigh it with your reasons. A ten-minute, do-it-yourself way to include your gut.

modalities.name: Weekly Felt Step
modalities.tagline: Each week, one small step the body proposes, then checked together.
modalities.whatItIs: Weekly Felt Step is a new concept that takes Focusing in the opposite direction from open, instruction-free meditation: more structure, a partner and more willingness to change something. Each week you meet one practice partner, let a felt sense propose one small real-life step, try it, and check next time how it felt.
modalities.coreIdea: Change may stick better when each step is chosen by the body and then felt again afterwards, in a steady weekly loop.
modalities.whatYouDo: You and a partner, both taught the format by a Focusing teacher, meet for an hour a week and take 30-minute turns. Each turn starts by sensing how last week's step felt, then lets a felt sense of the current situation form, asks "what small step would feel right?" and ends with that step written down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who gain insight easily but struggle to turn it into action, and who like a clear routine with one steady partner.
modalities.cautions: Steps should be small and safe, and old patterns that surface may need a therapist rather than a peer partner. It is an untested idea, not a substitute for treatment, and either partner can pause the arrangement at any time.
modalities.tweet: Insight but no action? Weekly Felt Step is a new idea: once a week with one partner, you check how last week's small step felt, then let your body propose the next one. A slow, structured loop from feeling to doing.

modalities.name: Room for Mixed Feelings
modalities.tagline: Let love and resentment sit side by side, unresolved.
modalities.whatItIs: Room for Mixed Feelings is a speculative practice that moves Focusing away from meditations that build one warm feeling. Instead of growing goodwill, you sense the whole tangle of a situation in the body, such as love and resentment together, and let both be there without resolving them.
modalities.coreIdea: Many situations feel two ways at once, and allowing the mixed bodily sense, instead of forcing one pleasant feeling, may be more honest and less tiring.
modalities.whatYouDo: Bring to mind a person or situation you feel torn about and, for about 20 minutes, notice where each feeling sits in the body. A quiet companion can sit with you and only say back what you name, and you end by acknowledging that both feelings are present, with nothing decided.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel guilty about having mixed feelings toward family, partners or work, and want a gentle way to let them be.
modalities.cautions: Sitting with conflicted feelings about close people can stir grief or anger, so keep sessions short and stop if it becomes overwhelming. If a relationship involves abuse or danger, safety and professional support come first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Love and resentment at the same time? New concept: Room for Mixed Feelings. Instead of trying to feel only kindness, you notice where each feeling sits in your body and let both stay. For anyone torn about someone close.

modalities.name: One Chapter, One Feeling
modalities.tagline: Feel a whole period of your life at once, then title it.
modalities.whatItIs: One Chapter, One Feeling is a new concept that pushes Focusing away from precise, structured observation of sensations and toward meaning and story. You take a whole period of your life, such as a year, a job or a move, and let a single felt sense of that chapter form while a friend listens.
modalities.coreIdea: A chapter of life can be felt all at once as a bodily whole, and finding words or images for it may clarify what that time meant.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trusted listener, spend 30 to 40 minutes on one chapter: name it, let its overall felt sense form, then let images, titles or phrases come and check each against that sense. The listener reflects back only your words, and afterwards you write a short title for the chapter.
modalities.whoItsFor: People at a turning point, such as a breakup, a career change or a big birthday, who want to make sense of a period of their life.
modalities.cautions: Looking back over a hard period can stir grief or old pain, so choose a chapter you feel ready for and stop if you feel flooded. People with traumatic histories should do this with a qualified therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what does a whole year of your life feel like, all at once? One Chapter, One Feeling has you sense one chapter (a job, a move, a relationship) as a single bodily feeling and find its title, with a friend listening.

modalities.name: First Minutes Awake
modalities.tagline: Before the phone and the day's thinking, sense how you are.
modalities.whatItIs: First Minutes Awake is a speculative practice that moves Focusing as far as possible from bursts of intense effort, into the calmest moment of the day. In the first minutes after waking, still lying down and before any screen, you let a felt sense form of how you are and of the day ahead, while dream fragments and old moods are still near.
modalities.coreIdea: Just after waking, before the busy mind takes over, feelings that are usually drowned out may be easier to sense.
modalities.whatYouDo: When you wake, stay lying down with your eyes closed for 10 minutes, with the phone out of reach. Let a felt sense of how you are and of the coming day form, welcome any image or mood left from the night without analyzing it, and jot one word on a bedside notepad before you get up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose days start at full speed with messages and news, and who want a quiet, self-led check-in before that happens.
modalities.cautions: Waking moods can be heavy, so if you regularly wake with dread or very low mood, talk to a doctor or therapist. Do not use it as a reason to stay in bed when that makes you feel worse; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: What if you sensed how you are before your phone tells you? First Minutes Awake: stay lying down for ten minutes after waking, let the feeling of the day ahead form, jot one word, then get up. A new idea for full-speed mornings.

modalities.name: Slow Ink Pages
modalities.tagline: Alone with a notebook, writing a feeling slowly, word by word.
modalities.whatItIs: Slow Ink Pages is a speculative practice that moves Focusing far from teams, noise and competition, into complete solitude on the page. Alone and seated, you write very slowly from a felt sense, letting images and memories appear in the writing.
modalities.coreIdea: Writing alone, at the speed of the felt sense, can give a vague feeling the time and privacy to find its words.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone with a notebook for 30 minutes, let the felt sense of one situation form, and write only what comes from it, a few words at a time, pausing to check each phrase against the feeling. Nobody reads it, and you can keep it, throw it away or reread it in a week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Introverts and people who think better on paper, or who have no listening partner but want to explore what they feel.
modalities.cautions: Writing about the past can bring up painful memories, so stop if you feel flooded and bring lasting distress to a therapist. It is an untested concept, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: An idea for people who think better on paper: Slow Ink Pages. Alone with a notebook, you let a vague feeling form and write only what comes from it, a few words at a time. No audience, no team, no hurry.

modalities.name: The Felt Sense of Enough
modalities.tagline: Feel, in the body, the moment something is enough.
modalities.whatItIs: The Felt Sense of Enough is a new concept that takes Focusing away from the more miles, more minutes spirit of endurance training. With guidance from a Focusing teacher, you learn to sense in the body the moment when work, effort or achievement is enough, and to listen to old messages that say it never is.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people have no felt sense of enough, only of not yet, and finding that signal may make it easier to stop at the right point.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a weekly 45-minute session with a Focusing teacher, and in short practices at home, you recall something you keep doing more of, such as working late or rewriting an email, and ask "what would enough feel like?". You wait for the body's answer, notice any old voice that says it is never enough, and the next time you are in that situation you pause to check for the felt signal.
modalities.whoItsFor: Overworkers, perfectionists and people who never feel they have done enough.
modalities.cautions: Old messages about never being enough can stir painful memories, so take them to a therapist if they keep coming up. A drive that feels out of control, or lasting exhaustion, deserves professional support; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Never quite feel it's enough? An idea: The Felt Sense of Enough. With a teacher's help, you learn to feel in your body the moment when work or effort is enough, and notice the old voice saying it never is. New and untested.

modalities.name: Soft Spot Company
modalities.tagline: Keep your tired, tender places company, with nothing to improve.
modalities.whatItIs: Soft Spot Company is a speculative practice that moves Focusing as far as possible from building strength and tracking progress. You turn kindly toward the places where you feel weak, tired or tender and keep them company without trying to make them stronger.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting weakness and tenderness be felt, rather than overcome, may ease the strain of always having to be strong.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down for 20 minutes and ask where in your body or your life you feel soft, tired or fragile right now. Rest your attention there as you would sit with a tired friend, let images or memories come if they do, and set no goal and keep no record.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are always the strong one, or who push through everything, and want a gentle, self-led way to let themselves be tired.
modalities.cautions: Old hurts can surface when you turn toward tender places, so go slowly, stop if it becomes too much and see a therapist if painful feelings persist. Tiredness that does not lift can have medical causes worth checking with a doctor; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Always the strong one? New concept: Soft Spot Company. Lie down, find where you feel tired or tender, and keep that place company, with no goal of getting stronger and nothing to track. An idea for people who push through everything.

modalities.name: The Shy Guest Wait
modalities.tagline: Leave an inner door open and wait warmly for what arrives.
modalities.whatItIs: The Shy Guest Wait is a new concept that takes Focusing away from contact with a real companion and toward a solitary, imagined relationship with your own inner sense. You picture the felt sense as a shy guest who arrives in its own time, and your only job is to wait warmly.
modalities.coreIdea: Treating a hard-to-reach feeling like a shy guest, rather than chasing it, may let it show itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: Alone, sit for 15 to 20 minutes, picture leaving a door open inside you and wait without searching. If something shows up, a sensation, an image or a word, greet it, let it stay as long as it likes and do not question it; if nothing comes, the waiting itself was the practice.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find that their feelings go quiet the moment they look for them, and who want a self-led practice with no pressure.
modalities.cautions: Waiting in silence can bring unexpected feelings or memories, so keep the right to stop, and get support from a therapist if they are distressing. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for care.
modalities.tweet: Feelings that hide when you look for them? Proposed practice: The Shy Guest Wait. Picture leaving a door open inside you and wait, warmly, for whatever wants to show up. No chasing, no questions. An idea to try on your own.

modalities.name: Kitchen Table Felt Sense
modalities.tagline: Pause mid-conversation to ask how it feels, and actually wait.
modalities.whatItIs: Kitchen Table Felt Sense is a speculative practice that moves Focusing away from set forms and formal sessions into ordinary conversation. Friends or family agree that, while talking over tea or a meal, any of them can pause and ask "how does that feel in you?" and wait for the answer.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner listening does not need a ritual; a shared habit of pausing in everyday talk can bring the felt sense into daily life.
modalities.whatYouDo: Agree on the habit with one or two people you talk with regularly. When someone speaks about something that matters, another asks how it feels in them, both pause for a few breaths while the speaker checks inside, and the conversation carries on, sometimes in a new direction.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like the idea of inner listening but will never sit down for a formal session, and households that want warmer conversations.
modalities.cautions: Not every moment suits inner questions, so anyone can decline, and the habit should never be used to pressure or analyze someone. Serious distress needs proper support; this is an untested idea, not therapy.
modalities.tweet: Speculative idea: Kitchen Table Felt Sense. Over tea or dinner, friends can pause and ask "how does that feel in you?" and actually wait. No formal session, no technique. Just slower, warmer conversations at home.

modalities.name: Six Regions in Order
modalities.tagline: Visit six body regions in order and map how you are.
modalities.whatItIs: Six Regions in Order is a new concept that takes Focusing away from social contact and into a quiet, structured solo routine. Lying alone, you visit regions of the body in a set order and let a small felt sense form in each one, building a private map of how you are.
modalities.coreIdea: Each part of the body can hold its own felt sense of your life, and visiting them in a set order may reveal patterns that a single check misses.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the routine from a teacher, lie down alone for 30 minutes and move through six regions (feet and legs, belly, chest, throat, face, back), asking each "what is the sense here about my life right now?". Write one word per region, and over the weeks look back at how the map changes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who need solitude to recharge and like a calm, orderly practice they can do alone.
modalities.cautions: This is not a medical check, so new or persistent pain needs a doctor. Some body areas can hold painful associations, so skip any region that feels unsafe, and people with trauma or dissociation should work with a qualified therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: New concept for people who recharge alone: Six Regions in Order. Lying down, you visit six body regions in order and ask each what it senses about your life now, then write one word per region. Over weeks, a private map appears.

modalities.name: Last Week, Day by Day
modalities.tagline: Recall each day of last week and feel which one holds most.
modalities.whatItIs: Last Week, Day by Day is a speculative practice that moves Focusing indoors, into memory and into a set routine. Once a week, seated at home, you recall each of the past seven days in turn, let a small felt sense of each one form, and then stay longer with the day that holds the most.
modalities.coreIdea: A week leaves a bodily trace day by day, and walking through it in order may show which moment still needs attention.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the routine from a Focusing teacher, sit for 30 minutes each Sunday and spend two minutes on each day from Monday on, picturing it and noting one word for its felt sense. Then return to the day that felt fullest and give it ten minutes of open Focusing, noticing any older memory it stirs without exploring it alone.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose weeks blur together and who like a regular, orderly reflection they can do at home.
modalities.cautions: A hard week can bring up strong feelings, and a day that keeps linking to old pain is worth taking to a therapist. It is an untested concept, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Weeks blurring together? Proposed practice: Last Week, Day by Day. Each Sunday, recall each day in turn, note one word for how it felt, then stay with the day that holds the most. A new, orderly way to reflect at home.

modalities.name: Between Us Sensing
modalities.tagline: Feel the sense of a relationship and find words for it.
modalities.whatItIs: Between Us Sensing is a new concept that takes Focusing away from raw sensory contact and toward the imagined space between you and another person. With a listener, you bring a relationship to mind, let the felt sense of "how it is between us" form and then find words for it.
modalities.coreIdea: Every relationship has its own felt sense, and naming it carefully may show what you want or fear in that relationship.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a trained listener, spend 45 minutes on one relationship: picture the person, notice the bodily sense of being with them and find a word or image that fits. If it echoes older relationships, notice that gently, and end by naming one thing you now know about what you want.
modalities.whoItsFor: People puzzling over a friendship, family tie or partnership who want to understand their own side before talking with the other person.
modalities.cautions: Exploring close relationships can stir old attachment pain, so go slowly and stop when you need to, and people with trauma histories should work with a qualified therapist. If a relationship is abusive or unsafe, contact support services; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Confused about where you stand with someone? Between Us Sensing is a proposed practice: picture the person, feel the sense of how it is between you, and find words for it with a listener. A way to understand your own side first.

modalities.name: Finding Your Own Tempo
modalities.tagline: Sense the pace your body wants, and compare it with your calendar.
modalities.whatItIs: Finding Your Own Tempo is a new concept that moves Focusing away from music, with its shared, imposed rhythms, toward the body's own pace. Lying quietly alone, you let a felt sense form of the speed at which you actually want to live today, and compare it with the speed your schedule demands.
modalities.coreIdea: Much strain may come from living at a tempo the body does not choose, and sensing the gap can show where life needs to slow down or, sometimes, speed up.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie down for 20 minutes in a quiet room and ask "what pace does my body want today?", waiting for a felt answer such as slow and heavy or quick and light. Then picture your calendar for the day, notice the felt sense of its pace, let the difference between the two be felt, and note one place where you could follow your own tempo.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel rushed, out of step with their schedule, or always a beat behind or ahead.
modalities.cautions: Constantly feeling too slow or too fast can reflect fatigue, low mood or other health issues worth discussing with a doctor. It is an untested idea, and some demands cannot change, so be kind to yourself about what you can adjust.
modalities.tweet: Living at someone else's tempo? New concept: Finding Your Own Tempo. Lie down, sense the pace your body wants today, then feel the pace of your calendar and notice the gap. One small change, chosen by feel.

modalities.name: Open-Eyed Presence Meetings
modalities.tagline: Meet a coach eyes open, in the real room, right now.
modalities.whatItIs: Open-Eyed Presence Meetings is a new concept that pushes Aletheia Coaching away from structured imagery work and toward plain contact in the present. Coach and client sit facing each other with eyes open, and the session stays with what is actually here: the room, the light, each other's faces and the feelings that arise between them.
modalities.coreIdea: Being fully seen and present with another person, in real time and without inner images, may itself let held-back feelings soften.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute one-to-one session, you sit across from a trained coach, eyes open, and describe what you notice in the room, in your body and in being looked at kindly. There is no set sequence, and when memories or images pull you away, the coach gently invites you back to what you can see and feel now.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who get lost in their heads or in the past and want a slow, warm practice of being present with another person.
modalities.cautions: Being looked at closely can feel exposing or stir old shame, so you can look away, pause or ask for more distance at any time. It is an untested idea offered as coaching, not therapy, so people with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should work with a qualified mental health professional.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Open-Eyed Presence Meetings. You sit with a coach, eyes open, and stay with what is actually here: the room, your body, being kindly seen. No imagery, no script. For people who live in their heads or in the past.

modalities.name: Your Posture, Mirrored
modalities.tagline: A coach quietly mirrors how you sit and breathe as you talk.
modalities.whatItIs: Your Posture, Mirrored is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from inner parts and imagined figures and toward what can be seen and sensed right now. As you talk, the coach gently mirrors your posture, gestures and breathing, so you can meet the way you hold yourself from the outside, calmly and without analysis.
modalities.coreIdea: Seeing your own way of holding yourself reflected by another person may make feelings you carry in the body easier to notice and allow.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute one-to-one session with a trained coach, you talk about something on your mind while the coach softly copies how you sit, where your hands go and how fast you breathe. Every so often you pause, look, notice what you feel on seeing it, and let that feeling be there without trying to change your posture.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find inner imagery or parts work abstract and learn best from what they can see.
modalities.cautions: Being mirrored can feel exposing or awkward at first, so you can ask the coach to stop at any time. This is an untested coaching idea, not therapy, and people with severe trauma, body image distress or a current crisis should work with a qualified mental health professional.
modalities.tweet: Ever seen how you actually sit when you talk about something hard? New concept: Your Posture, Mirrored. A coach quietly copies your posture and breathing so you can meet yourself from the outside. Untested, calm, no analysis.

modalities.name: When the Body Is Done
modalities.tagline: Deep sessions that end when the body feels complete, not the clock.
modalities.whatItIs: When the Body Is Done is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching as far as possible from structured, time-limited, agenda-led therapy. Sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care have no agenda and no fixed end: old feelings are allowed to move through the body, and the session ends when the body itself feels settled.
modalities.coreIdea: Old emotional material may need to finish its own arc, and letting the body's sense of completion mark the end may avoid stopping halfway.
modalities.whatYouDo: You book a half-day block with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, and lie or sit comfortably while noticing what the body brings up, with the therapist reflecting what you notice and checking that you feel steady. When a wave of feeling has passed and the body feels quiet, you both agree the session is done, whether that took 50 minutes or two hours.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who often feel cut off mid-feeling by the end of a 50-minute session and want deep work at the body's pace.
modalities.cautions: Open-ended deep work can be intense, so it belongs only with a licensed clinician experienced in trauma, with breaks, a firm outer time limit and a plan for staying grounded afterwards. It is an untested concept, not suitable during a crisis, and not a replacement for well-tested treatments for PTSD or depression.
modalities.tweet: Ever been cut off mid-feeling when a session hits 50 minutes? New concept: When the Body Is Done. Deep work with a trauma-trained therapist that ends when your body feels settled, not when the clock says so. An untested idea.

modalities.name: Regrets, Felt Through
modalities.tagline: Meet old regrets in the body, without turning them into lessons.
modalities.whatItIs: Regrets, Felt Through is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from values work, action plans and the present moment, toward the past choices you regret. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you let a regret be felt in the body without having to repair it, learn from it or plan anything.
modalities.coreIdea: Regret is often rushed into lessons or pushed away, and simply letting it be felt, with steady company, may let it soften on its own.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 75-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you bring one regret, from a recent choice to something from long ago, and describe the moment slowly. You notice where the regret sits in the body and what younger feelings it touches, while the therapist keeps the pace bearable and never asks for a lesson or a plan.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who replay old choices, carry guilt about the past, or have been told too often to "just move on".
modalities.cautions: Regret can bring up shame, grief or self-blame, so this belongs with a licensed clinician experienced in trauma, at a pace you control. If regret comes with thoughts of suicide or self-harm, seek urgent professional help; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Replaying a choice you regret? Regrets, Felt Through is a proposed practice: with a trauma-trained therapist, you let a regret be felt in your body without turning it into a lesson or a plan. A new idea for people told to just move on.

modalities.name: Busy Hands, Slow Talk
modalities.tagline: Talk about what matters while your hands knead, sort or wind.
modalities.whatItIs: Busy Hands, Slow Talk is a new concept that moves Aletheia Coaching away from intense, symptom-focused uncovering and toward calm, sideways attention. While your hands do something simple, such as kneading clay, sorting beans or winding yarn, you and a coach talk slowly, and feelings are allowed to come up at the edge of attention rather than head-on.
modalities.coreIdea: With the hands calmly occupied, hard topics may feel less exposing and feelings may surface more gently.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute sessions, you sit at a table with a simple hand task while a trained coach sits beside you rather than opposite. You talk about whatever is on your mind, and when a feeling stirs the coach invites you to notice it in the body, keep your hands moving and let it be.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who freeze up in face-to-face talk, or who feel calmer when their hands are busy.
modalities.cautions: Coaching is not therapy, so severe distress, trauma symptoms or a crisis need a qualified mental health professional. It is an untested idea; choose materials that suit any allergies or hand problems.
modalities.tweet: Freeze up in face-to-face talks? Busy Hands, Slow Talk is a new idea: you knead clay or sort beans while talking with a coach who sits beside you, so feelings can come up sideways. Untested, calm and low pressure.

modalities.name: Two Voices, One Room
modalities.tagline: Two people speak from feeling while a clinician guides both.
modalities.whatItIs: Two Voices, One Room is a speculative practice that takes Aletheia Coaching away from body exercises and toward words, images and relationship. Two people who share a history, such as partners, siblings or old friends, take turns speaking from their feelings while a licensed therapist trained in trauma care guides both.
modalities.coreIdea: Speaking from feeling, rather than about it, in front of someone who matters may help both people understand the old patterns between them.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 90-minute sessions led by a licensed therapist trained in trauma care and in couple or family work, each person in turn speaks slowly from what they feel about a shared situation, using images and memories as they come, while the other only listens and then says back what they heard. The therapist keeps the pace slow, interrupts blaming and helps each person stay with their own experience.
modalities.whoItsFor: Pairs who keep having the same painful conversation and want a slow, guided way to hear each other's inner experience.
modalities.cautions: Working with shared history can stir old hurts, so it needs a licensed clinician trained in trauma and in couple or family work, and it is not suitable where there is violence, coercion or fear of the other person. It is an untested concept, not a replacement for couples therapy when that is needed.
modalities.tweet: Same painful conversation, again and again? New concept: Two Voices, One Room. Two people take turns speaking from their feelings, not about them, while a trauma-trained therapist keeps it slow. An idea for partners, siblings and old friends.

modalities.name: Words on Loan
modalities.tagline: The therapist offers tentative words; you check if they fit.
modalities.whatItIs: Words on Loan is a speculative practice that pushes Aletheia Coaching away from self-help methods in which you find your own words. A licensed therapist trained in trauma care offers tentative words for what you might be feeling, especially about old experiences, and you check each one against your inner sense, keeping only what fits.
modalities.coreIdea: Some feelings, especially from early life, never got words, and trying on offered words, with full freedom to reject them, may help them be named.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 60-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you speak about something that troubles you and the therapist now and then offers a phrase such as "I wonder if it felt lonely" or "maybe there is anger there too". You pause, feel whether it fits, answer "yes", "not quite" or "no", and the therapist never insists or suggests what happened.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who struggle to name feelings, or who grew up in families where feelings were not talked about.
modalities.cautions: Offered words can be suggestive, so this belongs only with a licensed clinician trained in trauma care who is careful never to lead you toward memories or conclusions. It is an untested concept, not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Can't find words for what you feel? Words on Loan is a new concept: a trauma-trained therapist offers tentative words, and you check each against your gut, keeping only what fits. For people who grew up where feelings went unnamed.

modalities.name: Six-Seat Unfolding Circle
modalities.tagline: A small group, a clear format and guided deep inner work.
modalities.whatItIs: Six-Seat Unfolding Circle is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from open, instruction-free meditation and toward a structured small-group format. Six people meet with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care and group work, and each takes guided turns at slow, feeling-based exploration while the group listens with full attention.
modalities.coreIdea: Being witnessed by a small, steady group, within a clear and safe format, may deepen inner work that feels lonely one to one.
modalities.whatYouDo: The circle meets for three hours every two weeks over six months; each meeting opens with ten minutes of shared silence, then two or three people take a 30-minute turn led by the licensed therapist trained in trauma care, while the others hold quiet attention. Each turn ends with listeners saying one thing they felt while witnessing, without advice or analysis.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want depth work but also want to feel less alone in it, and who like a reliable format.
modalities.cautions: Group depth work can stir strong feelings and shame, so the therapist leading it must be a licensed clinician trained in trauma and group work, members should be screened beforehand, and anyone can pass. It is an untested idea and not suitable for people in crisis.
modalities.tweet: An idea for doing deep inner work without feeling alone: the Six-Seat Unfolding Circle. Six people, a trauma-trained therapist, guided turns and a group that listens without advice. New, untested, and built on a clear, safe format.

modalities.name: Unsweetened Feeling Sessions
modalities.tagline: Hard feelings may stay hard, and someone witnesses them.
modalities.whatItIs: Unsweetened Feeling Sessions is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from meditations that build warm, positive feelings. Grief, anger, envy or despair are met in the body and allowed to stay exactly as they are, without being turned into compassion or goodwill, while a licensed therapist trained in trauma care keeps you company.
modalities.coreIdea: Feelings that are always softened or reframed may never be fully felt, and letting them stay unsweetened, with support, may let them run their course.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute one-to-one sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you name a hard feeling, find where it lives in the body and let it be felt at a pace the therapist helps keep bearable, while they reflect what they notice. You can bring a trusted friend to sit in silently, and you never have to forgive, reframe or find a lesson.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel pushed to be positive, forgiving or grateful and want a place where hard feelings are allowed.
modalities.cautions: Strong grief or anger can be overwhelming, so sessions belong only with a licensed clinician trained in trauma, with a steady pace and time to settle before leaving. If anger comes with urges to harm anyone, or despair with thoughts of suicide, tell your therapist at once or contact emergency services; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Tired of being told to look on the bright side? Unsweetened Feeling Sessions is a new concept: grief or anger is felt in the body and allowed to stay as it is, with a trauma-trained therapist beside you. No forced forgiveness, no lessons.

modalities.name: Lifelong Daydreams
modalities.tagline: Explore the daydreams you have returned to since childhood.
modalities.whatItIs: Lifelong Daydreams is a new concept that moves Aletheia Coaching away from precise sensory observation and toward the private fantasies you have carried for years. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you explore a recurring daydream, such as being rescued, admired or far away, and feel what longing it holds.
modalities.coreIdea: Daydreams that return across a lifetime may carry old, unmet needs in picture form, and feeling into them may show what they have been asking for.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, one to one or in a small group of three screened people, you describe in the present tense a daydream you have had since childhood or youth. You pause on its most charged moment, notice what you feel in the body and what need it seems to serve, and the therapist asks only open questions.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who notice the same fantasies returning and are curious about what they say.
modalities.cautions: Daydreams can touch grief and early hurts, so this needs a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, and group members must be screened. Daydreaming that takes over many hours a day deserves a professional assessment; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Have a daydream you've returned to since childhood? Lifelong Daydreams is a proposed practice: with a trauma-trained therapist, you explore what longing it holds and what it's been asking for. An untested, imaginative idea.

modalities.name: At Half Speed
modalities.tagline: Deep inner work done at half the pace of ordinary talk.
modalities.whatItIs: At Half Speed is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching as far as possible from fast, intense effort. Everything in the session happens at half the usual pace, with long pauses after every sentence, so that deep and old feelings are only ever approached slowly and in stillness.
modalities.coreIdea: Radical slowness may be what makes deep material bearable: at half speed there is always time to notice, settle and choose whether to go on.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma, you sit or lie very still, and both of you speak in short phrases separated by long pauses. Whenever something old or painful stirs, the therapist slows things down further and checks that you feel steady before you stay with it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who talk fast, rush past their feelings or feel flooded when deep material comes too quickly.
modalities.cautions: Slowness lowers but does not remove the intensity of deep work, so it needs a licensed clinician experienced in trauma and a pace you can stop at any time. It is an untested idea, not suitable during a crisis, and not a replacement for well-tested trauma treatment.
modalities.tweet: New concept: At Half Speed. Deep inner work where everything happens at half the usual pace, with long pauses after every sentence and a trauma-trained therapist beside you. An idea for people who rush past their own feelings.

modalities.name: Guided Cabin Solitude
modalities.tagline: Days alone in a quiet place, with one guided talk a day.
modalities.whatItIs: Guided Cabin Solitude is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching away from teams, games and constant company into deep solitude. You spend a few days alone in a quiet place, letting inner images and old feelings come in their own time, and meet a licensed therapist trained in trauma care once a day to make sense of what arose.
modalities.coreIdea: Long stretches of solitude can let deep feelings surface that never appear in a busy week, and a daily meeting with a therapist gives a regular place to make sense of them.
modalities.whatYouDo: For three to five days you stay alone in a simple retreat cabin with your phone switched off and put away, spending the days resting, sitting, writing and noticing images, memories and moods. Each day you have a one-hour session with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care who stays nearby, and the cabin has a landline or emergency phone so you can reach them at any hour.
modalities.whoItsFor: Experienced inner explorers, not in crisis, who want an extended, solitary stretch of depth work with a safety net.
modalities.cautions: Solitude and intensive inner work can bring up difficult experiences, including fear, panic or unreal feelings, so a licensed clinician trained in trauma should screen participants first, and people with a history of psychosis, mania, dissociation or severe trauma should not do this without their clinician's agreement. It is an untested idea, and you can end the stay early at any time.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: three days alone in a quiet cabin, no phone, letting old feelings surface in their own time, with a daily talk with a trauma-trained therapist. Guided Cabin Solitude, an untested idea for experienced inner explorers.

modalities.name: The Long Interval
modalities.tagline: One deep session, then weeks for life to do its part.
modalities.whatItIs: The Long Interval is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from steady, sustained effort and toward deliberate gaps. Deep sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care are spaced a month or more apart, with no homework in between, because the time between sessions is treated as part of the work.
modalities.coreIdea: What shifts in a deep session may need weeks of ordinary life to settle, so spacing sessions widely puts rest, not persistence, at the center.
modalities.whatYouDo: Every four to six weeks you have a 90-minute session with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, where you slowly feel into what has been stirring and let it be met. Between sessions you do nothing special, apart from a short check-in message two weeks later and the option to call if something difficult comes up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who cannot manage weekly sessions, feel overloaded by homework, or prefer to let things settle in their own time.
modalities.cautions: Deep material opened in one session can stir things up in the weeks that follow, so it belongs only with a licensed clinician trained in trauma care who is reachable between sessions. It is an untested idea and not suitable for anyone in crisis or needing regular treatment.
modalities.tweet: What if the weeks between sessions were part of the work? An idea: The Long Interval. One deep session with a trauma-trained therapist every month or so, no homework, and time for life to let things settle. A new concept for people who feel overloaded.

modalities.name: Old Words About Your Body
modalities.tagline: Explore what you were told about your body growing up.
modalities.whatItIs: Old Words About Your Body is a new concept that moves Aletheia Coaching as far as possible from building and shaping the body, toward the words that shaped how you see it. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you recall what family, teachers or peers said about your body when you were young, and feel how those words still sit in you.
modalities.coreIdea: Early comments about size, strength or looks can become lasting beliefs, and meeting them slowly in words and feeling may loosen their grip.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 60-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you bring one remembered remark, such as "you're the weak one" or "you'll never be sporty", say it aloud and notice the feeling and memory that come with it. There is no exercise, weighing or mirror work, and the therapist never asks you to change how you look.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry old shame or harsh beliefs about their bodies and want to understand where they came from.
modalities.cautions: Body-related memories can touch bullying, abuse or disordered eating, so this needs a licensed clinician trained in trauma, and anyone with an eating disorder should work within their own treatment team. It is an untested idea, not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: "You're the weak one." Words about your body can last decades. Old Words About Your Body is a proposed practice: with a trauma-trained therapist, you revisit what you were told and feel how it still sits in you. A new idea.

modalities.name: Childhood Rooms Revisited
modalities.tagline: A guided imagined walk through the rooms you grew up in.
modalities.whatItIs: Childhood Rooms Revisited is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from outward contact with real companions and toward inner imagery of the past. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you imagine walking through the rooms of a home you grew up in and notice the felt sense each room brings.
modalities.coreIdea: Places hold feelings, and slowly revisiting remembered rooms in imagination may bring old emotional learnings gently into awareness.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute sessions, a licensed therapist trained in trauma care invites you to picture the front door of a childhood home and move at your own pace from room to room, describing what you see and feel in the body. You choose which doors to open and can step back outside at any moment, and the therapist never suggests what you should find.
modalities.whoItsFor: People curious about how their early home shaped their feelings today, who think easily in pictures.
modalities.cautions: Imagery of childhood can bring up painful memories, and imagined scenes are not a reliable record of what happened, so this needs a licensed clinician trained in trauma who avoids leading questions. People with severe trauma, dissociation or a current crisis should only do it as part of their own treatment; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Places hold feelings. Childhood Rooms Revisited is a proposed practice: with a trauma-trained therapist, you imagine walking through the home you grew up in, room by room, choosing which doors to open. A new idea, done slowly.

modalities.name: Names You Were Given
modalities.tagline: Explore the nicknames and labels you grew up with.
modalities.whatItIs: Names You Were Given is a new concept that moves Aletheia Coaching away from body forms and toward the words that shaped you. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you explore nicknames, labels and family descriptions from childhood, such as "the clever one" or "the difficult one", and feel how each still lands in you.
modalities.coreIdea: Labels given early can become quiet rules about who we are, and feeling each one may loosen its hold.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before the first session you list names and labels you were called growing up, kind and unkind. In 60-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you say one aloud, pause, notice the feeling and any memory it brings, and sense whether it still fits you today.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel boxed in by an old family role or a label from school.
modalities.cautions: Hurtful names can bring up shame or memories of bullying or abuse, so this belongs with a licensed clinician trained in trauma care, at your pace. It is an untested idea, not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: "The clever one." "The difficult one." Which labels did you grow up with? Names You Were Given is an untested idea: with a trauma-trained therapist, you say each one aloud and feel how it still lands in you.

modalities.name: The Untold Story Room
modalities.tagline: Do deep work without ever telling what happened.
modalities.whatItIs: The Untold Story Room is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from sharing and social connection and toward complete privacy. You never have to say what happened: you bring a memory to mind privately and report only what you notice in your body, while a licensed therapist trained in trauma care helps you stay steady.
modalities.coreIdea: Some experiences are too private or painful to put into words, and working only with the body's response may let them be met without being told.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 60-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma, you lie or sit comfortably, silently recall something that still troubles you, and say only words like "tight chest" or "warmth in my hands". The therapist guides you to notice those sensations, pause and settle, following a simple, repeatable routine.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry experiences they cannot or will not describe, or who feel exposed by talking.
modalities.cautions: Recalling painful memories, even silently, can be intense, so this belongs only with a licensed clinician experienced in trauma, who will check how steady you feel throughout. It is an untested idea and not a replacement for well-tested trauma treatment.
modalities.tweet: Some things are too private to say out loud. The Untold Story Room is a new concept: you recall a memory silently and report only what you feel in your body, while a trauma-trained therapist keeps you steady. Your story stays yours.

modalities.name: Keepsake in Hand
modalities.tagline: Bring an object from your past and let it lead you back.
modalities.whatItIs: Keepsake in Hand is a speculative practice that moves Aletheia Coaching indoors and deep into personal history through a single object. You bring a keepsake, such as a toy, a letter or a piece of jewelry, and a licensed therapist trained in trauma care helps you let its feeling lead you, step by step, into what it holds.
modalities.coreIdea: Objects kept for years can hold whole periods of feeling, and attending to one slowly may open the way to old emotional memories at a manageable pace.
modalities.whatYouDo: In each 75-minute session with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you follow the same steps: describe the object, hold it and notice the body's response, let one memory come, then put the object down and return to the present room. You decide how far to go, and the therapist helps you pause whenever the feeling grows too strong.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who keep things from their past and sense those objects mean more than they can say.
modalities.cautions: Keepsakes can carry grief or painful memories, so this needs a licensed clinician experienced in trauma, and you can leave the object outside the room at any time. It is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Kept something from your past for years? Proposed practice: Keepsake in Hand. Bring the object to a trauma-trained therapist, hold it, let it lead you slowly into what it holds, then set it down again. A new idea.

modalities.name: Stories We Inherited
modalities.tagline: Explore the family stories you grew up inside.
modalities.whatItIs: Stories We Inherited is a new concept that takes Aletheia Coaching away from sensory, present-moment work and toward the family stories that shaped you. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you explore the tales, sayings and unspoken rules passed down in your family and notice how each one still feels in you.
modalities.coreIdea: Family stories carry emotional lessons across generations, and feeling into them may show which ones you still live by.
modalities.whatYouDo: In 75-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you recall stories and sayings you heard growing up, such as "we don't make a fuss" or the tale of a grandparent's hardship, and let images and feelings come. Later, you can invite a parent, sibling or other relative to one session to share their version, if both of you want to.
modalities.whoItsFor: People curious about how family history, migration or hardship still echoes in their own reactions.
modalities.cautions: Family stories can touch painful or traumatic history, and joint sessions with relatives can stir conflict, so this needs a licensed clinician trained in trauma and family work, and relatives should never be pressured to attend. It is an untested idea, not a replacement for therapy.
modalities.tweet: "We don't make a fuss." Which family sayings still run your life? Stories We Inherited is a proposed practice: explore the stories you grew up inside, with a trauma-trained therapist, and notice how each one still feels. A new idea.

modalities.name: The Held-Back Feeling
modalities.tagline: Explore how you learned to hold back, without forcing release.
modalities.whatItIs: The Held-Back Feeling is a new concept that moves Aletheia Coaching away from music, singing and open expression and toward restraint itself. With a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you explore the bodily feel of holding back tears, words or anger, and where you learned to, without any push to let it out.
modalities.coreIdea: Holding back was once protective, and feeling the holding itself, rather than forcing release, may let it relax when it is ready.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly 60-minute sessions with a licensed therapist trained in trauma care, you notice where you hold back in the body, such as a tight throat or a clenched jaw, and let a memory of when that began come into view. The therapist helps you stay with the holding gently and never asks you to cry, shout or perform a release.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who cannot cry or speak up when they want to, and who are wary of methods that push for catharsis.
modalities.cautions: Old reasons for holding back can be painful or traumatic, so this needs a licensed clinician experienced in trauma and a pace you control. It is an untested idea and not suitable during a crisis.
modalities.tweet: Can't cry, or swallow your words? The Held-Back Feeling is a proposed practice: with a trauma-trained therapist, you explore the tight throat or clenched jaw itself, and where it began, with no push to let it all out.

modalities.name: Idle Eyes at the Window
modalities.tagline: Sit at a window, eyes open, and let looking happen.
modalities.whatItIs: Idle Eyes at the Window is a new concept that pushes Do Nothing meditation further from imagery-based therapy, toward the plain outside world. You sit at a window with your eyes open and let looking happen by itself, with no instruction from anyone, no inner pictures to build and no history to explore.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting the eyes wander over the real world, without steering them or building inner images, may be one of the simplest ways to rest the mind.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose a window, sit down for 10 to 20 minutes and let your gaze go wherever it goes: clouds, a wall, passing cars, a fly. If you notice yourself trying to look properly or to meditate well, let that go too, and get up whenever you like.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find eyes-closed meditation strange or heavy and want a no-instruction rest they can start on their own today.
modalities.cautions: Open sitting can still let worries or difficult feelings surface; if that keeps happening, try a more guided practice or talk to someone you trust. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for anxiety or depression.
modalities.tweet: New idea: Idle Eyes at the Window. Sit at a window, eyes open, and let your gaze wander over clouds, walls and passing cars. No instructions, no visualizing, nothing to get right. A rest you can start today if eyes-closed meditation feels strange.

modalities.name: Unanswered Inner Chatter
modalities.tagline: Your running inner commentary keeps talking; you stop answering it.
modalities.whatItIs: Unanswered Inner Chatter is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from therapies that hold conversations with inner parts. When your ordinary running commentary worries, judges or argues, you neither answer it, nor argue back, nor try to quiet it; you let it talk like a radio in another room.
modalities.coreIdea: Inner chatter may lose some of its pull when nobody inside answers it, so not replying becomes a way to rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or lie down for 15 minutes with your eyes open or closed and let sounds, sensations and the running commentary in your head all happen. Each time you catch yourself replying to a thought, reassuring it or arguing with it, drop the reply and let the commentary carry on unanswered.
modalities.whoItsFor: People with busy, chattering minds who are tired of arguing with their own thoughts.
modalities.cautions: If you hear voices that seem to come from outside you, or that frighten or command you, stop and speak with a doctor or mental health professional. It is an untested idea, and people with psychosis, severe trauma or dissociation should not use it in place of professional care.
modalities.tweet: An idea for chattering minds: Unanswered Inner Chatter. When your ordinary running thoughts worry or argue, you don't answer, argue back or shush them. You let them talk like a radio in the next room. For anyone tired of arguing with themselves.

modalities.name: Hammock, Nothing Else
modalities.tagline: Lie in a hammock, let it sway, and add nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Hammock, Nothing Else is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation even further from structured, scheduled therapy. You lie in a hammock, indoors or in a garden, let it sway or settle as it will, and add nothing: no timer, no technique, no book, no music.
modalities.coreIdea: A hammock holds and gently rocks the body without any effort, which may make letting go of control feel natural rather than like a task.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie in a securely hung hammock and let your body be rocked or still, with whatever thoughts, sounds and drowsiness come and go. Do not set a timer or keep a record; climb out when you feel like it, slowly, with both feet on the ground first.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find sitting meditation stiff or effortful, and anyone who rests best when held and rocked.
modalities.cautions: Hang the hammock securely at a low height and get in and out carefully, since falls are the main risk, and skip it if you have dizziness or balance problems. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for stress or sleep problems.
modalities.tweet: Find sitting meditation stiff? New concept: Hammock, Nothing Else. Lie in a hammock, let it sway or settle, and add nothing: no timer, no technique, no book, no music. Climb out when you feel like it.

modalities.name: Nothing, Side by Side
modalities.tagline: Two people in one room, both doing nothing, no talking.
modalities.whatItIs: Nothing, Side by Side is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from therapy built on conversation, values and plans. Two people who are at ease with each other sit in the same room and both do nothing, without talking, looking after each other or doing anything together.
modalities.coreIdea: Quiet company that asks nothing may make doing nothing feel less lonely or strange, without turning it into a shared activity.
modalities.whatYouDo: Agree with a partner, friend or housemate on 20 minutes, sit in the same room in any comfortable position, and each let whatever happens happen. There is no rule about eye contact, no sharing afterwards and no need to stay if one of you wants to stop.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find solo meditation lonely, and couples or friends who are always busy together and rarely just are together.
modalities.cautions: Choose someone you feel safe and relaxed with, and stop if the silence starts to feel tense. It is an untested idea, not a treatment, and difficult feelings that surface deserve support from someone you trust or a professional.
modalities.tweet: Always busy together, never just together? An idea: Nothing, Side by Side. You and a friend or partner sit in the same room for 20 minutes, both doing nothing, no talking, no sharing afterwards. Untested, and oddly cozy.

modalities.name: The Sun Patch
modalities.tagline: Rest in a patch of sunlight, like a cat.
modalities.whatItIs: The Sun Patch is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation far from intense, therapist-led work on hidden emotional meaning, toward simple warmth and light. Whenever sunlight falls into a room, you sit or lie in the patch it makes and do nothing until it moves on.
modalities.coreIdea: Warmth and light are among the simplest comforts, and resting in them with nothing to work on may let the body settle on its own.
modalities.whatYouDo: On a sunny day, find where light falls through a window, sit or lie in it with your eyes open or closed and let whatever happens happen. Stay as long as it feels pleasant, or until the patch has moved off you, and then get on with your day.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who spend most of the day indoors, and anyone who wants a no-skill, no-equipment way to rest.
modalities.cautions: Sunlight through glass can still burn and overheat you, so keep sessions short in strong sun, drink water and never look straight at the sun. It is an untested idea and not a substitute for care when low mood or anxiety persists.
modalities.tweet: Ever envied a cat in a sunbeam? The Sun Patch is a new idea: when sunlight falls into a room, sit or lie in it and do nothing until it moves on. No skill, no app, no equipment. Just warmth.

modalities.name: Worry Left Unsolved
modalities.tagline: Let one worry sit there, untouched, for ten minutes.
modalities.whatItIs: Worry Left Unsolved is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from body-based release methods and toward the mind. A worry is allowed to sit in your thoughts while you neither solve it, nor soothe it, nor try to release it through the body; you simply let it be there.
modalities.coreIdea: Many worries grow when we keep trying to settle them, and leaving one unsolved for a few minutes may show that it can be tolerated.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit for 10 minutes, bring to mind a current worry and then stop doing anything about it: no planning, no reassuring, no breathing techniques. When the mind starts problem-solving, let the attempt drop and let the worry sit there like an unopened letter.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who solve, plan or reassure themselves endlessly and want to practice letting a worry be.
modalities.cautions: If worry is constant, overwhelming or stops you sleeping or functioning, it may be an anxiety problem that deserves professional help. It is an untested idea, and real problems still need practical action at another time.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: let one worry sit there, unsolved, for ten minutes. No planning, no reassuring, no breathing tricks. Worry Left Unsolved is a new idea for people who can't stop problem-solving in their heads.

modalities.name: Phoneless Café Table
modalities.tagline: Sit at a busy café with a drink and nothing else.
modalities.whatItIs: Phoneless Café Table is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from quiet, inward listening to the body and out among people. You sit at a café table with a drink, with no phone, book, laptop or company, and let the life of the place go on around you while you do nothing.
modalities.coreIdea: Doing nothing in public, silently alongside strangers, may show that rest does not need a quiet room or closed eyes.
modalities.whatYouDo: Order something, leave the phone in your bag and sit for 20 minutes with your eyes open. Let conversations, clatter, people passing and your own thoughts come and go, and if you notice an urge to look busy or to watch people on purpose, let that go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they can only rest at home, and anyone who reaches for a phone the moment they sit down in public.
modalities.cautions: Keep an eye on your belongings, and choose a calm café if crowds make you anxious. It is an untested idea, and if being alone in public brings strong anxiety or low mood, talking to a professional may help.
modalities.tweet: Sit down in a café and reach straight for your phone? An idea: Phoneless Café Table. A drink, no phone, book or laptop, and 20 minutes letting the clatter and chatter go on around you while you do nothing. New and untested.

modalities.name: Threshold Pauses
modalities.tagline: At every doorway you pass, pause for a breath of nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Threshold Pauses is a speculative practice that takes Do Nothing meditation away from long guided sessions and deep work, and ties it to one everyday place: the doorway. Each time you step through a door at home or work, you pause on the threshold for a few seconds and let whatever is happening happen.
modalities.coreIdea: Doorways mark the shift from one task to the next, and a few seconds of not controlling anything there may stop one activity's tension spilling into the next.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose the doors you pass most, such as your front door, office door or bathroom door, and pause on each threshold for a slow breath or two, dropping any effort to steer your attention. There is nothing to learn and no teacher, and then you simply walk on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Busy people who never find time to meditate, and anyone who carries one meeting or chore into the next.
modalities.cautions: Do not stop in doorways where people or traffic need to pass, and never pause like this on stairs or while carrying something heavy. Short pauses are not a treatment for mental health problems; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Carry one task's stress into the next? New concept: Threshold Pauses. Each time you step through a door, pause on the threshold for a breath or two and let whatever is happening happen, then walk on. No app, no teacher.

modalities.name: Welcome the Boredom
modalities.tagline: Let dull, ordinary time stay dull, and stay with it.
modalities.whatItIs: Welcome the Boredom is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from practices that build up warm, pleasant feelings. Instead of cultivating goodwill or bliss, you welcome the flat, dull, boring moments that most meditation tries to get past.
modalities.coreIdea: Boredom is usually escaped within seconds, and letting it be, without making it pleasant, may make ordinary life easier to sit with.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit somewhere unremarkable for 15 minutes with no phone, music or book, and let the time feel as dull as it does. When you notice an urge to make it nicer (a pleasant thought, a plan, a fidget), let the urge be and stay with the plain, flat feel of the moment.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who reach for their phone at every quiet moment and want to get comfortable with ordinary, unexciting time.
modalities.cautions: Feeling flat for a few minutes is normal, but a lasting loss of interest or pleasure can be a sign of depression that deserves a talk with a doctor. It is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Reach for your phone in every quiet moment? Welcome the Boredom is a new idea: fifteen minutes somewhere unremarkable, no phone or music, letting the time feel as dull as it is. No bliss to chase, just ordinary time. 📵

modalities.name: Fog Allowed Sitting
modalities.tagline: When the mind is hazy, let it stay hazy.
modalities.whatItIs: Fog Allowed Sitting is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from insight practices that observe experience precisely. You make no attempt to see clearly: when the mind is foggy, vague or half-dreaming, you let it stay that way.
modalities.coreIdea: Demanding clarity of a tired mind can become its own strain, so allowing the fog may let rest happen.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or recline for 15 to 20 minutes, close your eyes or let them unfocus, and let thoughts be blurry and half-formed. You do not label, note or examine anything, and if you notice an effort to see more clearly, you drop it and let the haze be.
modalities.whoItsFor: Tired people, and meditators who feel they must always be alert and precise, who want a gentler, hazier rest.
modalities.cautions: Fogginess that lasts, or new trouble thinking clearly, can have medical causes and should be checked by a doctor. This untested idea is not for moments that need alertness, and people with dissociation should talk to a clinician before trying it.
modalities.tweet: Mind too foggy to meditate? Fog Allowed Sitting is a proposed practice that says fine, stay foggy. No noting, no examining, no effort to see clearly, just letting a hazy mind rest. A new concept for tired brains.

modalities.name: Parked Car Pause
modalities.tagline: Engine off, before you go inside: a few minutes of nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Parked Car Pause is a new concept that takes Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from intense, timed effort, into the quiet gap between parts of the day. When you arrive home or at work by car, you stay put for a few minutes with the engine off and do nothing before going in.
modalities.coreIdea: The minutes between one role and the next are usually skipped, and spending them doing nothing may let the mind arrive more fully.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once you are safely parked with the engine off, put the phone in the glove box, sit back and let thoughts about where you have been and where you are going come and go for three to ten minutes. Then get out and go in, with nothing to report or record.
modalities.whoItsFor: Commuters and parents who rush straight from work into the next demand and want a small buffer.
modalities.cautions: Only do this when properly parked in a safe, well-lit place with the engine off, never on a road shoulder and never in a closed garage with the engine running. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for stress.
modalities.tweet: Rushing from work straight into the next demand? New idea: the Parked Car Pause. Engine off, phone in the glove box, and three to ten minutes of doing nothing before you walk in the door. A small buffer between roles.

modalities.name: The Unreachable Half Hour
modalities.tagline: Thirty minutes when nobody can need anything from you.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unreachable Half Hour is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from teams, roles and constant coordination with others. For thirty minutes you make yourself completely unreachable, with phone off and door closed, and do nothing at all.
modalities.coreIdea: Knowing that nobody can call on you, even briefly, may let the part of the mind that is always on standby switch off.
