modalities.whatYouDo: Tell anyone who depends on you that you will be unavailable for half an hour, switch your phone off (not just to silent) and close the door. Sit or lie however you like and let whatever happens happen, until the half hour is over.
modalities.whoItsFor: Parents, carers, managers and anyone who is always on call and rarely has time that belongs to nobody else.
modalities.cautions: Only do this when someone else is covering anyone who needs supervision, such as young children or a person you care for. Solitude can let low mood surface, so if it regularly leaves you feeling worse, talk to someone; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: For parents, carers and anyone on call, an idea: The Unreachable Half Hour. Phone off (not on silent), door closed, someone else covering, and thirty minutes when nobody can need anything from you. Untested, but easy to try.

modalities.name: Nowhere to Get To
modalities.tagline: Turn queues, platforms and waiting rooms into rest.
modalities.whatItIs: Nowhere to Get To is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from steady effort toward a distant goal. It uses the moments when you are stuck waiting, in queues, on platforms or in waiting rooms, as a chance to stop trying to get anywhere and let whatever happens happen.
modalities.coreIdea: Waiting is usually spent straining toward what comes next, and dropping that strain may turn dead time into rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Learn the idea from a short guide or book, then each time you have to wait, leave your phone in your pocket and stop willing the wait to end. Let your eyes, thoughts and impatience do whatever they do, and when the bus, the queue or the appointment arrives, simply carry on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Impatient people, commuters and anyone who loses a lot of time to waiting and finds it irritating.
modalities.cautions: Stay aware of your surroundings, your belongings and any traffic, and never do this while driving or cycling. It is an untested idea, and impatience that comes with intense anger or anxiety may deserve professional support.
modalities.tweet: Stuck in a queue again? New idea: Nowhere to Get To. Each time you have to wait, phone stays in your pocket and you stop willing the wait to end. Let thoughts and impatience do what they do. Dead time, turned into rest.

modalities.name: Beside the Undone List
modalities.tagline: Sit next to your to-do list and do nothing about it.
modalities.whatItIs: Beside the Undone List is a speculative practice that takes Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from effort, progress and achievement. You sit near your unfinished tasks, with the to-do list in plain view, and for a set while you do nothing about any of them.
modalities.coreIdea: Resting while tasks remain undone, rather than only after they are finished, may loosen the belief that rest has to be earned.
modalities.whatYouDo: Put your to-do list on the table, sit beside it for 15 minutes and let thoughts about deadlines, guilt and plans come and go without acting on them. When the urge to tick something off appears, let it be an urge, and when the time is up, go back to work normally.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they can only rest once everything is done, which is never.
modalities.cautions: This is not a way to ignore urgent deadlines, bills or safety tasks, so deal with those first. If overwhelm or procrastination is seriously affecting your life, it may help to talk to a doctor or therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Think you have to earn your rest? Beside the Undone List is a new concept: sit next to your to-do list for 15 minutes and do nothing about any of it. Let the guilt and urges come and go. An idea for people who are never done.

modalities.name: Lights Out, Nothing Doing
modalities.tagline: In bed with the lights off, stop trying to fall asleep.
modalities.whatItIs: Lights Out, Nothing Doing is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from contact with a living companion, toward the dark, solitary minutes before sleep. Once the light is off, you do nothing at all, including trying to fall asleep, and let thoughts, pictures and drowsiness come and go.
modalities.coreIdea: Trying hard to fall asleep is itself a kind of effort, and dropping it, along with every other effort, may make the minutes before sleep feel less like a task.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each night, once the light is off and the phone is away, lie in any comfortable position and let whatever happens happen. If you notice an intention to relax, to empty your mind or to get to sleep, let it go too, and if you are still wide awake after a long while, get up and do something calm.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who lie in bed fighting their thoughts or trying hard to sleep.
modalities.cautions: This is not a treatment for insomnia: if poor sleep lasts for weeks or affects your days, talk to a doctor, since well-tested help exists. It is an untested idea, and if lying in the dark brings up distressing memories, keep a soft light on and seek support.
modalities.tweet: Lying in bed trying hard to fall asleep? An idea: Lights Out, Nothing Doing. Once the light's off, do nothing at all, not even trying to sleep, and let thoughts and drowsiness come and go. Untested, and no substitute for help with insomnia.

modalities.name: Slumped and Unposed
modalities.tagline: No posture, no breathing technique: rest exactly as you are.
modalities.whatItIs: Slumped and Unposed is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from careful postures and regulated breathing. You sit or sprawl in whatever position you happen to be in, slumped on the sofa if that is where you are, and leave the breath and body alone entirely.
modalities.coreIdea: Arranging the body and breath can quietly turn rest into a performance, so leaving them unarranged may remove one more layer of control.
modalities.whatYouDo: Wherever you are sitting or lying, stop for 10 to 20 minutes without straightening up, closing your eyes or adjusting your breath. Let attention drift through thoughts and daydreams, and when you catch yourself fixing your posture or breathing deeply on purpose, let that go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel they cannot meditate because they cannot sit still or upright, and anyone put off by strict postures.
modalities.cautions: Shift position if something starts to ache or go numb, since leaving the body alone does not mean staying in pain. It is an untested idea, and anyone with breathing problems or chronic pain should follow their own clinician's advice.
modalities.tweet: Good news for sofa sprawlers. Slumped and Unposed is a new idea: stay exactly as you are, leave your breath and posture alone, and let your mind drift. No performance, no technique.

modalities.name: Talk-Free Evening
modalities.tagline: An evening of not speaking after a socially full week.
modalities.whatItIs: Talk-Free Evening is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation as far as possible from talk and social contact. After days full of people, you spend an evening alone without speaking, messaging or listening to talk, and simply let the quiet be.
modalities.coreIdea: Speech keeps the social mind running, and a stretch of not talking at all may let it wind down more fully than ordinary rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once you have learned the idea from a short guide, pick an evening, tell the people you live with, and put away your phone and anything with voices in it. Move slowly through ordinary things like making tea or lying on the bed, and in between, sit and do nothing until bedtime.
modalities.whoItsFor: Introverts, people in people-heavy jobs and anyone who feels talked out by the end of the week.
modalities.cautions: Make sure someone can still reach you in an emergency, and do not use silence to avoid people you need to talk to. If you avoid company because of fear or low mood, or the quiet makes you feel worse, talk to a doctor or therapist; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: A week full of people? New concept: the Talk-Free Evening. No speaking, no messaging, no podcasts, just moving slowly through tea and quiet and doing nothing until bed. An untested idea for introverts and people in people-heavy jobs.

modalities.name: Snug Corner Pause
modalities.tagline: Tuck yourself into a small, sheltered corner and do nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Snug Corner Pause is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from open landscapes and walking, into a small, enclosed indoor space. You set up a snug corner, such as a window seat, a deep armchair with a blanket or a gap between shelves, and go there only to do nothing.
modalities.coreIdea: A small, sheltered space can feel protective, and keeping one spot just for doing nothing may make it easier to stop.
modalities.whatYouDo: After reading a short guide, choose and arrange your nook with a cushion and a blanket, and visit it for 15 minutes when you need a break. Inside, you let thoughts, daydreams and sounds come and go without steering them, and you keep phones, books and work out of the nook.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find open spaces or bare rooms hard to relax in, and anyone who loved dens and cozy corners as a child.
modalities.cautions: Enclosed spaces can feel uncomfortable for people with claustrophobia, so keep the nook open on one side and leave whenever you like. It is an untested idea, not a treatment for anxiety.
modalities.tweet: Loved building dens as a kid? Proposed practice: Snug Corner Pause. Set up a snug corner with a cushion and blanket, keep phones and work out, and go there only to do nothing for 15 minutes. A new idea for cozy minds.

modalities.name: After the Last Page
modalities.tagline: When a story ends, stay with its echo before moving on.
modalities.whatItIs: After the Last Page is a speculative practice that moves Do Nothing meditation away from the senses and into the imagination a story leaves behind. When you finish a book, film or episode, you do not reach for the next one; you sit for a while doing nothing and let the story's images and feelings linger or fade on their own.
modalities.coreIdea: Stories leave an afterglow that is usually cut short by the next thing, and staying with it without steering may be a rest in itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: After reading a short guide, close the book or switch off the screen at the end, stay seated and keep the room quiet for 10 minutes. Scenes, characters and feelings may replay, drift or vanish, and you neither analyze them nor push them away; then you get up and carry on.
modalities.whoItsFor: Readers and viewers who binge one story after another and rarely let any of them land.
modalities.cautions: Sad or frightening stories can leave you low or unsettled, so if the afterglow is distressing, turn on a light, move around or talk to someone. It is an untested idea, not a treatment.
modalities.tweet: Finish one episode, start the next? New concept: After the Last Page. When a book or film ends, stay seated for ten quiet minutes and let its scenes and feelings linger or fade on their own. An idea for bingers.

modalities.name: Unmasked Everyday Noise
modalities.tagline: Stop masking everyday noise: hear it and do nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Unmasked Everyday Noise is a new concept that moves Do Nothing meditation away from music and toward the plain, unmasked sound of daily life. Instead of covering traffic, neighbors or office hum with music or podcasts, you take the headphones off, sit, and let ordinary noise be heard while you do nothing.
modalities.coreIdea: Many of us mask the world's sounds all day, and letting them in, unedited and unchosen, may make daily noise feel less like something to escape.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a day, in a place with ordinary background noise, take off your headphones, put the phone away and sit for 10 to 15 minutes. Let sounds you like and sounds you do not like come and go, along with any irritation they bring, without reaching for anything to cover them.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who wear headphones most of the day and find everyday noise hard to bear.
modalities.cautions: Do not do this in places with harmfully loud noise, and protect your hearing where volume is high. If sounds feel unbearable or trigger distress, it may be sound sensitivity worth discussing with a doctor; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Headphones in all day to block the world out? An idea: Unmasked Everyday Noise. Ten minutes a day sitting with ordinary noise, traffic, neighbors, office hum, unmasked, while you do nothing. A new concept for noise-weary ears.
